title: Is it getting worse?
question: By the year an agreement was first approved, what share later grew by a quarter or more, and how large are the increases the Board approves each year?
finding: Of agreements first approved by the Board in 2014 to 2018, 11 of 121 (9%) grew by a quarter or more within three years; of those first approved in 2019 to 2023, 6 of 88 (7%). The later group is not higher. What has clearly risen is the volume of amendments: the Board passed 27 amendments a year to these agreements in 2014 to 2018 and 58 a year in 2021 to 2025. Those that state the amount before and after (110 and 268 of them) added $1.82 billion and $6.13 billion in those five-year spans. The typical single increase was 40% of the ceiling before it in the first span and 64% in the second.
how: Board of Supervisors titles from 2014 to 2026 were linked into one record per agreement, following only links proven by a dollar figure carried from one title to the next or by a shared contract number (the rule used in the amendment-growth screen). The first amount is the total in the first approval on file or, where the first file is an amendment, the amount that amendment says it started from; the latest is the highest total approved. Left out: 527 leases and property; 225 no usable name in the title; 167 agreements with other public bodies; 164 no amount in any title; 58 loans; 21 agreements that bring money in (concessions, rents, franchises). Two measures by year. First, for agreements whose first approval is on file: the share whose ceiling reached a quarter above the first amount through amendments introduced within three years of the first file (years after 2023 have not had three years). Second, for every amendment that states the amount before and after: how many increases the Board approved in the year they were introduced, the dollars they added, and the typical increase as a share of the ceiling before it. The comparison of the two groups uses a one-sided exact test.
limits: The first measure rests on a few dozen agreements a year and only on those large enough to go to the Board at the start. The second counts amendments, and more agreements may now cross the $10 million line simply because prices and programmes have grown; the years 2020 to 2022 also produced emergency agreements that were then enlarged. A rise in amendments is also what a policy of extending existing providers rather than re-bidding would look like, which is a choice the Board made case by case in public. The contract table cannot supply a trajectory because it holds no history. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
